transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Lately I keep forgetting everyday things I’m supposed to do, like taking my pills or bringing what I need to church events, even when I write them down. It has become a lot more noticeable over the last couple of years, especially since retiring and losing my husband left my days so unstructured. It's quite embarrassing, so my primary doctor recommended I come speak with you.
Did these memory and concentration problems start after your husband’s death or retirement, or had they already been going on before then? Also, have they been steadily worsening over time?

They’ve gotten steadily worse and much harder to manage over the last two years since my husband passed and I retired, but I actually had similar struggles dating all the way back to childhood. Even in grade school, my teachers would note on my report cards that I daydreamed too much, forgot my homework, and talked out of turn. The lack of structure in my days recently has just made these lifelong issues much more noticeable.
Before your husband passed away and before you retired, did these attention and forgetfulness problems cause trouble at work, home, or in relationships for most of your life?

No, for most of my adult life, I actually had a reputation for being very reliable, especially when I was working and my husband was alive. It's really only been over the last couple of years, with my schedule becoming so unstructured, that these issues have started causing real trouble in my daily life and relationships.

Did your attention and forgetfulness problems cause clear difficulties in school or daily life consistently from childhood through adulthood, or did they mainly become a problem only after your husband’s death and retirement?

While I had some of those tendencies back in grade school—like my teachers saying I daydreamed too much or talked out of turn—they didn't cause major difficulties during my adult years. It was only after my husband passed and I retired, leaving my schedule completely unstructured, that these issues truly became a disruptive problem in my daily life.

Before your husband passed away and you retired, did you still have these attention or forgetfulness problems in a way that caused clear difficulties at work, home, or in relationships for most of your life, or did they only become a real problem after that recent stress and change in routine?

They only became a real problem after that recent change in my routine. Throughout my adult life and career, I managed quite well and was actually known for being highly reliable. It wasn't until my husband passed and I retired, leaving my days completely unstructured, that these issues started causing real difficulties.

Before your recent loss and retirement, did you have ongoing problems with inattention or impulsivity that caused clear difficulties in more than one area of life since childhood, or did those symptoms mostly appear only after the change in your routine and stress?

Back in grade school, it did cause some trouble with teachers moving my seat for talking too much or complaining about my daydreaming. But throughout my adult life, I managed to keep it under control, and it only became a real, disruptive problem after my routine changed so much recently.

Before age 12, did you have ongoing attention, impulsivity, or hyperactivity problems that caused clear difficulties at home and school, and did those problems continue to affect you in more than one area of life as an adult?

Yes, back in grade school my report cards always mentioned that I daydreamed, forgot to turn in homework, and talked out of turn so much they had to move my seat. Now, these issues are definitely affecting multiple areas of my life, as people at church and my volunteer groups no longer trust me with important tasks. Even my daughter has started double-checking my plans because she worries I'll mess up the grandkids' schedules.

Did these attention and forgetfulness problems clearly begin or significantly worsen only after your husband’s death and retirement, or were they already causing persistent problems across school, work, and home long before that?

They definitely worsened and became a real problem only after my husband passed and I retired because I lost all my structure. However, I actually had similar struggles dating all the way back to childhood, like in grade school when teachers noted I daydreamed, forgot homework, and talked out of turn. It's just that they didn't cause persistent problems in my adult life until my routine changed so much recently.

When you were working and had a structured routine, did you still have ongoing attention or impulsivity problems that caused clear difficulties in more than one area of life, or were those symptoms mostly manageable until your husband died and you retired?

They were mostly manageable during my working years because having a highly structured routine really kept me on track. It was only after my husband passed and I retired, leaving my days completely unstructured, that these difficulties became prominent and started interfering with my daily life.

Did these memory and concentration problems begin within a few months after your husband’s death and retirement, and have they been tied mainly to that stress and change in routine? Or do you feel they are independent of the loss and have continued even when your days are structured?

These focus and memory issues aren't entirely new, as I struggled with daydreaming, forgetting homework, and talking out of turn back in grade school. However, losing my husband and retiring took away the structure that kept me on track, making these lifelong patterns much harder to manage over the last two years. So while the sudden lack of routine made things much worse, the underlying tendencies have actually been there my whole life.
When your days are structured, do the attention and forgetfulness problems mostly improve, or do they stay just as disruptive even with a routine?

Having a structured routine back when I was working really kept me on track, and losing that structure made things much worse. Now, even when I try to create my own routine using phone alarms and lists on the fridge, the forgetfulness and distractions still disrupt my day.
Do you also have symptoms of hyperactivity or impulsivity, such as feeling restless, fidgeting, interrupting others, or acting before thinking?

Yes, I definitely do. During church services or meetings, I constantly fidget by tapping my foot or fiddling with my keys because of a pent-up, jittery feeling inside. I also struggle with interrupting, often jumping in to finish people's sentences or offering unprompted advice to my family and fellow volunteers before realizing I've stepped on their toes.
Have these attention, restlessness, or impulsive behaviors caused clear problems in at least two settings, such as at home, with family, at church, or in volunteer work, since childhood?

Yes, they have. Back in grade school, it caused trouble at school because I would daydream, forget my homework, and talk out of turn. Now, it causes problems at church where volunteers have stopped relying on me, and at home where my daughter has to double-check my schedule with the grandkids.
Do you often feel very restless or unable to sit still, and do you frequently interrupt others or act before thinking?

Yes, I do. When I have to sit still for a long time, like during church or meetings, I get a jittery, pent-up feeling that makes me tap my feet, fiddle with papers, and feel like I just have to keep moving. I also find myself jumping in to finish people's sentences or offering unsolicited suggestions to my family and fellow volunteers before realizing I’ve stepped on their toes.

Before age 12, were you noticeably hyperactive or impulsive at school or home, such as being unable to stay seated, running/climbing excessively, or constantly interrupting and acting without thinking?

Yes, back in grade school, my teachers wrote on my report cards that I "daydreamed too much" and forgot to turn in homework I’d actually finished. I also talked out of turn so much that they had to move my seat more than once, which was definitely a sign of that impulsivity.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview confirms a lifelong pattern beginning before age 12 with inattention, forgetfulness, and impulsive/hyperactive behaviors (daydreaming, forgetting homework, talking out of turn, fidgeting, interrupting). Symptoms are present in multiple settings and now cause clear functional impairment. Because hyperactive/impulsive symptoms are clearly endorsed in addition to inattention, the best fit is combined-type ADHD rather than predominantly inattentive type.
